newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan rebels say enter Kabul, defenders fleeing.
newsitem.headline: Afghan rebels say enter Kabul, defenders fleeing.

text.p: Afghanistan's rebel Taleban Islamic militia were on Friday reported to have captured parts of Kabul and the main government airbase as defending forces seemed to be abandoning the besieged capital.

Taleban sources in Pakistan said the militia seized the Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) north of the capital, late on Thursday night and had entered the Wazir Akbar Khan diplomatic district in central Kabul.

They said the Taleban, which already controls most of afghanistan and wants a strict Islamic order, earlier took the capital's disused Khwaja Rawash airport in the northeast and the Soviet-built Microrayon housing complex in the east.
The sources, quoted by the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) service, said militia troops loyal to President Burhanuddin Rabbani were fleeing northwards.
His militia were putting up resistance to the Taleban near the presidential palace in the centre of the capital.
There was no immediate independent confirmation of the report, which also said the Taleban had taken Kohe Asmai hill, known as Television Hill, in the middle of Kabul.
But witnesses in Kabul said government troops appeared to be abandoning the capital as rebel Taleban forces were poised on the edge of the city.
I drove shortly before nightfall through desolate streets virtually devoid of traffic. The security ministry building had been abandoned and stood empty.
Some civilians had fled the city on the road north earlier in the day in dozens of trucks and buses, but with a curfew in force most Kabul citizens stayed in their homes.
In the Wasir Akbar Khan diplomatic quarter, small groups of residents came onto the streets to burn posters of President Rabbani and his military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.
Earlier, a government spokesman told reporters in Kabul that government forces would fight to the death to defend the capital.
"We are establishing defences in every street of Kabul," said spokesman Amrullah as the two sides fought on in the city's outskirts.
"We are not short of ammunition, fuel, morale or motive. We will remain in Kabul whether we are on the earth or beneath it."
Amrullah said the Taleban had lost hundreds of men to reach the eastern outskirts of Pul-i-Charkhi "and will perhaps lose thousands in Kabul".

An official of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Jan-Luc Paladini, said there had been hundreds of dead and wounded on both sides in the past two days of fighting, but he had no details.
He said the ICRC had medical stocks in Kabul to last for six months and the ICRC relief department had been bringing more over the past few days.

The ICRC on Thursday stopped all flights from Bagram to the Pakistani city of Peshawar, fearing the military situation could worsen, after evacuating 50 people, including 16 ICRC delegates, leaving only staff needed for emergencies.
But Paladini said: "The ICRC is staying in Kabul. We are not leaving."
Amrullah accused Pakistan of sending military technicians to help the Taleban and said other countries, which he refused to name, were also aiding the rebels.
"We are defending the country's pride against Pakistani puppets. Pakistan wants to control our country. We are ready to give as much sacrifice as required. We don't mind if we die."
But Pakistan denied the accusations.
The 15-nation U.N. Security Council appealed for a ceasefire and peace talks after a meeting in New York on Wednesday.
